Reasoning

1. Molecular formula C₉H₁₁NO₂ (index of H-deficiency = (2C+2+N–H)/2 = (18+2+1–11)/2 = 5).  
   Five unsaturations correspond to a benzene ring (4) + one carbonyl (1).

2. IR spectrum  
   • 3420 cm⁻¹ and 3325 cm⁻¹ – two N–H stretches of a primary amine (–NH₂).  
   • 1720 cm⁻¹ – strong carbonyl band of an ester (amide C=O would appear lower, ≈1650–1690 cm⁻¹).

   So the molecule is an aromatic ester that also contains a primary amine.

3. ¹H-NMR spectrum  
   • 1.20 ppm (t, 3 H) and 4.5 ppm (q, 2 H) – an ethyl group bound through oxygen (–O-CH₂-CH₃), typical of an ethyl ester.  
   • 4.0 ppm (broad s, 2 H) – NH₂ protons.  
   • 7.0 ppm (d, 2 H) and 8.0 ppm (d, 2 H) – two doublets of equal area, the AA′BB′ pattern of a para-disubstituted benzene ring.

4. Comparison with the choices  
   A. 4-Aminophenyl propionate – has CH₃CH₂–CO–O–Ph; the CH₂ α-to-C=O would resonate near 2.3 ppm, not 4.5 ppm.  
   B. Ethyl 4-aminobenzoate – contains an ethoxy (O-CH₂CH₃) ester, a p-NH₂ group, and gives the required para-aromatic pattern.  
   C. N-(4-ethoxyphenyl)formamide – would show an aldehydic ¹H near 8–9 ppm and only one N–H proton, not observed.  
   D. 3-Ethoxybenzamide – has an amide carbonyl (IR ≈1650 cm⁻¹) and a meta-substituted ring (complex aromatic pattern).

Only option B fits all the spectral features.

Answer: B
